title: Time Prepositions: At, On and In
summary: Choose at, on or in to locate an event in time. Learn when to omit a preposition and how to say that something will happen a short time from now.
learningObjectives: Use at for clock times and common fixed time phrases.
Choose on for days, dates and named parts of a day, and in for months, years, seasons and general parts of a day.
Leave out at, on and in before time expressions beginning with this, last, next or every.
Use in with a length of time to say when a future event will happen.

explanation.heading: At: exact times and fixed phrases
explanation.body: Use at with clock times and with midnight. Other useful expressions are at night, at the weekend, at Christmas, at the moment and at the end of a period.
explanation.example: Our online meeting begins at half past nine.

explanation.heading: On: days, dates and specific day parts
explanation.body: Use on with days of the week and dates. Use on when morning, afternoon, evening or night is attached to a particular day: on Wednesday afternoon, on Saturday night.
explanation.example: The music class is on Thursday evening.

explanation.heading: In: months, years, seasons and daytime
explanation.body: Use in for months, years and seasons. For a general part of the day, say in the morning, in the afternoon or in the evening; the usual general expression for night is at night.
explanation.example: I often go cycling in the morning.

explanation.heading: No preposition with this, last, next or every
explanation.body: A time expression beginning with this, last, next or every normally stands alone. Do not add at, on or in before it.
explanation.example: We are visiting the new museum next Saturday.

explanation.heading: In: time remaining from now
explanation.body: Use in followed by an amount of time to say how soon a future event will happen. In twenty minutes means twenty minutes from now, not the duration of an activity.
explanation.example: The next bus will arrive in twenty minutes.

comparisons.title: A general time of day or a named day

left.label: General time
left.example: I usually cook in the evening.
left.note: In introduces the part of the day without a specific weekday.

right.label: Named day
right.note: On introduces the day together with its part of the day.

left.label: Ordinary weekday
left.note: Use on when a weekday stands alone.

right.label: Next weekday
right.note: Do not add on before next Friday.

examples.note: At marks a precise point in time.

examples.sentence: Our football team practises on Sundays.
examples.note: On is used with regularly occurring weekdays.

examples.sentence: Can we speak at the end of the lesson?
examples.note: At the end of is a fixed time expression.

examples.sentence: The taxi will be here in fifteen minutes.
examples.note: In fifteen minutes means fifteen minutes from now.

commonMistakes.why: Use in for a general part of the day.
Use on when night follows a named weekday.
Next already identifies the time, so omit the preposition.

studyTips: Group time expressions by size: at seven o’clock, on Friday, in July, in 2027.
Notice the contrast between in the evening and on Saturday evening.
Check the first word of a time phrase. This, last, next and every usually mean no at, on or in.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The appointment begins ___ 9:15.
exercises.feedback: Use at before a clock time such as 9:15.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: We visit our cousins ___ November.
exercises.feedback: Use in for months of the year.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The train arrives ___ Thursday evening.
exercises.feedback: A named weekday and its evening take on.
Next Tuesday needs no preposition before it.

exercises.prompt: Complete with at, on or in: My alarm rings ___ 6:40 every weekday.
exercises.feedback: Use at with a precise time.

exercises.prompt: Complete with at, on or in: The village festival takes place ___ October.
exercises.feedback: In is the preposition for a month.

exercises.prompt: Complete with at, on or in: Our lesson is ___ Wednesday morning.
exercises.feedback: Wednesday morning is a specific part of a named day, so use on.

exercises.prompt: Complete with at, on or in: The taxi will arrive ___ ten minutes.
exercises.feedback: In ten minutes means ten minutes from now.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We play basketball in Friday evenings.
acceptedAnswers: We play basketball on Friday evenings.
exercises.feedback: Use on before a named weekday plus evenings.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: My parents met on 2008.
Correct the sentence: The class starts in ten o'clock.
acceptedAnswers: The class starts at ten o'clock.
exercises.feedback: Use at for a clock time.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I am free on this weekend.
exercises.feedback: Do not use on before a time expression beginning with this.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the complete sentence with the correct preposition: 'The concert starts ___ seven thirty.'
acceptedAnswers: The concert starts at seven thirty.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use at before the clock time seven thirty.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the full sentence with the correct preposition: 'Our garden looks beautiful ___ spring.'
acceptedAnswers: Our garden looks beautiful in spring.

speakingExercises.prompt: Remove the unnecessary preposition and say the full sentence: 'We are visiting Clara on next Tuesday.'
acceptedAnswers: We are visiting Clara next Tuesday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Leave out on before next Tuesday.

speakingExercises.prompt: A sign shows that the pharmacy closing time is noon. Tell a visitor in one full sentence beginning 'The pharmacy closes ...'.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use at with noon, a specific time of day.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change the general morning to Friday morning. Say the new complete sentence, keeping the other words: 'We practise in the morning.'
speakingExercises.feedback: Use on for a named weekday and its morning, rather than in for a general morning.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend asks when the book fair is. The poster says October. Answer in one sentence beginning 'The book fair is ...'.
acceptedAnswers: The book fair is in October.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use in before the name of a month.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the prepositions in both sentences, keeping all other words, and say them in order: 'We sleep in night. We dance at Saturday night.'
acceptedAnswers: We sleep at night. We dance on Saturday night.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use at night for a general time, but on before Saturday night.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your train leaves twenty minutes from now. Tell a friend in one sentence, beginning 'The train leaves ...'.
acceptedAnswers: The train leaves in twenty minutes.
speakingExercises.feedback: In twenty minutes means twenty minutes from now, not a twenty-minute journey.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our family dinner is on Saturday evening.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which preposition is used before the named evening?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker uses on before Saturday evening, a named part of the week.

listeningExercises.audioText: I usually read in the afternoon.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which preposition comes before the general part of the day?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker uses in with the afternoon when no weekday is named.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the preposition you hear directly before midnight.
listeningExercises.feedback: At midnight marks a specific point in time.

listeningExercises.audioText: The school is closed on Monday, so the music lesson will be on Tuesday afternoon.
listeningExercises.prompt: When can students attend the music lesson?
listeningExercises.feedback: The school is closed on Monday; the lesson is scheduled for Tuesday afternoon.

listeningExercises.audioText: The swimming pool opens at eight. My lesson doesn't begin until eight forty.
listeningExercises.prompt: How long after the pool opens does the lesson begin?
listeningExercises.feedback: The pool opens at eight, and the lesson starts at eight forty: a forty-minute difference.

listeningExercises.audioText: We usually have music practice on Mondays, but there's no practice next Monday.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is true about the coming Monday's session?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker says that there is no practice next Monday, despite the usual Monday schedule.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children always eat their sandwiches at lunchtime, after playing outside.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single preposition immediately before the daily mealtime.
listeningExercises.feedback: At is used before lunchtime in this sentence.

listeningExercises.audioText: Your glasses will be ready in twenty minutes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single preposition that tells you how soon the glasses will be ready.
listeningExercises.feedback: In twenty minutes means twenty minutes from now.
